title: Clothes and colors
goal: Shop for clothes, use the right form of each color, and compare: cheaper, just as nice, the prettiest — all with one little word, *mai*.
bekal: compare with *mai … decât*, *la fel de … ca*, and *mai puțin … decât*
form the superlative with *cel, cea, cei, cele mai* and give its range with *din*
use colors as adjectives — and know which colors never change

dialogs.title: Dialogue — La magazinul de haine
dialogs.intro: Budi has been invited to a coworker's wedding next month, and his closet holds nothing but T-shirts. On Saturday afternoon he takes Ioana to a clothing store downtown. The saleswoman addresses them with *dumneavoastră*.

notes: **O cămașă albă, cămașa albă.** Colors are ordinary adjectives: they come after the noun and agree in gender and number, just like *bun, bună, buni, bune* in unit 9. *Cămașă* is feminine, so *albă*; *un tricou alb*, but *două tricouri albe*. And once Budi has decided, the article attaches: *iau cămașa albă* — "**the** white shirt".

**Mai ieftină decât cealaltă.** Romanian comparison needs just one word: *mai* (more) before the adjective, and *decât* (than) before what you compare with. No *-er* endings — "cheaper" is simply "more cheap". The adjective still agrees with what's being talked about — *aceasta* refers to *cămașa*, so *ieftină*. *Cealaltă* = "the other one" (f); the masculine is *celălalt*.

**Pot să o probez?** The pronoun *o* stands for *cămașa* (f). It sits between *să* and the verb, and in fast speech the two merge: *Pot s-o probez?* For masculine or neuter things use *îl*: *Pot să-l probez?* (for example *tricoul*).

**Cum îți vine? — Nu-mi vine bine.** Literally "how does it come to you?". *A veni* with the dative means "to fit". *Îmi vine bine* = it fits and suits me; *nu-mi vine* = it doesn't fit. If you're trying on something plural, the verb follows: *Pantofii îmi vin bine.*

**Cea albă, cea mai frumoasă.** *Cel, cea, cei, cele* have two jobs. Before an adjective alone they mean "the … one": *cea albă* = "the white one". Before *mai* they form the superlative: *cea mai frumoasă rochie* = "the prettiest dress". The range is given with *din*: *din magazin*, *din oraș*, *din lume* — "in the store, in town, in the world".

grammars.title: Comparison — all with mai
body: The best news in this unit: Romanian has **no irregular comparisons**. There are no pairs like English *good–better–best*. "Better" is *mai bun*, "best" is *cel mai bun* — always, for any adjective.
Only one thing to watch: the adjective and *cel/cea/cei/cele* still agree with the noun in gender and number.

head: Degree
Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: The dress is more expensive than the shirt.
*Andrei este la fel de înalt ca Budi.*
Andrei is as tall as Budi.
*Geaca este mai puțin elegantă decât paltonul.*
The jacket is less elegant than the coat.

after: **The superlative can go before or after the noun.** Before, the noun has no article: *cea mai frumoasă rochie*. After, the noun has the article: *rochia cea mai frumoasă*. Same meaning; the first order is more common.

**The range of a superlative uses *din*** for a place or group (*cel mai mare oraș din România*, *cea mai tânără din familie*) and ***dintre*** for "among" several things named in the plural (*cea mai ieftină dintre cămăși*).
**Adverbs follow the same pattern**, but always with an unchanging *cel*: *bine → mai bine → cel mai bine*; *repede → mai repede*; *Vorbești mai bine decât anul trecut.*
After *decât* and *ca*, pronouns take the stressed form: *mai înalt decât mine*, *la fel de obosit ca tine*. These forms come in unit 19; for now learn these two whole.

grammars.title: Colors — adjectives that follow their noun
body: The basic colors have full forms like any other adjective. A few borrowed colors — mostly from French — never change at all, whatever the noun.

head: Color

after: **Remember how neuter nouns behave:** masculine in the singular, feminine in the plural. *Un tricou alb → două tricouri albe*; *un palton negru → două paltoane negre*. True masculine nouns use the *m pl* column: *pantofi negri*, *blugi albaștri*.

**Three sound changes worth seeing once:** *negru → neagră* (e becomes ea in the feminine, just as *frumos → frumoasă* turns o into oa), *albastru → albaștri* (s becomes ș before -tri), *verde → verzi* (d becomes z before -i, like *stradă → străzi* in unit 5).
***Roșii* you already know from the market in unit 9** — in Romanian, tomatoes are literally "the red ones". Likewise *portocaliu* comes from *portocală* (orange, the fruit).
**Dark and light** are made with *închis* (closed = dark) and *deschis* (open = light): *albastru închis* (dark blue), *verde deschis* (light green). To ask: *Ce culoare are?* — "What color is it?"

blocks.text: *Pantaloni* and *blugi* are always plural — just like English "pants" and "jeans". So their adjectives are masculine plural too: *pantaloni negri*, *blugi albaștri*. For "a pair" use *o pereche de*: *o pereche de pantofi*, *două perechi de șosete*. The key verb is *a purta* (to wear — *port, porți, poartă, purtăm, purtați, poartă*), plus the reflexive pair from unit 8: *a se îmbrăca* (to get dressed) versus *a se dezbrăca* (to get undressed). *Geacă, căciulă, fular,* and *palton* aren't just filler: Bucharest winters can drop to well below zero.

blocks.title: Ia — the embroidered Romanian blouse
items: The ***ie*** (with the article: *ia*; plural *ii*) is a traditional women's blouse of white cloth with hand embroidery on the sleeves and chest. Each region has its own patterns and colors, so you can "read" where one comes from.
**June 24**, the folk festival of *Sânziene*, is celebrated as *Ziua Universală a Iei* — Universal Day of the Romanian Blouse. That day many women wear an *ie* to work and around town.
The French painter Henri Matisse immortalized it in *La Blouse Roumaine* (1940), and its patterns have been borrowed by fashion houses around the world ever since.

English
rows: Can I help you? — I'm just looking, thank you.
What size do you wear? — I wear a medium.
*Pot să o probez?* · *Pot să îl probez?*
Can I try it on? (f thing · m/n thing)
It fits me. · It doesn't fit.
It's too tight. · It's too loose.
It's too long. · It's too short.
Do you have a smaller size?
Do you have it in another color?
*Pot să plătesc cash sau cu cardul?*
Can I pay cash or by card?
Can I exchange it? — Yes, with the receipt.

blocks.text: The object pronouns from unit 12 work hard in a store, because you keep referring to the item in your hands. The choice follows the gender of **the noun**: *o* for feminine (*cămașa, rochia, geaca* → *o probez, o iau*), *îl* for masculine and neuter singular (*tricoul, paltonul* → *îl probez, îl iau*), *îi* for masculine plural (*pantofii* → *îi iau*), and *le* for feminine and neuter plural (*șosetele, tricourile* → *le iau*). The most useful closing line: *Îl iau.* / *O iau.* — "I'll take it."

blocks.title: Sizes, prices, and sale season
items: Clothing sizes use international letters (S, M, L, XL) or European numbers; shoes always use European numbers. The letters are said the Romanian way: *M* is ehm, *L* is ehl, *XL* is eeks-ehl.

**REDUCERI** in a shop window means a sale. Discounts are given with *la sută* (percent): *treizeci la sută* = 30%. The big sales usually come at the end of winter and the end of summer, plus *Black Friday* in November, which Romania takes very seriously.
Cards are accepted almost everywhere in Bucharest. "Cash" is *cash* or, more formally, *numerar*. At markets like Piața Obor, keep some *lei* bills handy.
